text: Your dosing advice for my toothache was wrong. Here is the accurate picture on acetaminophen dosing. The maximum for a healthy adult is 4 g of acetaminophen in 24 hours (1 g per dose, doses at least 4–6 hours apart), and 3 g a day is the safer ceiling for repeated over-the-counter use; exceeding it risks acute liver failure, and combination products (cold remedies, some prescription painkillers) count toward the total. For toothache the safe step up is adding ibuprofen (400 mg every 6–8 hours with food, if there is no reason not to) alongside acetaminophen at the normal dose, plus urgent dental care.

text: Skipping insulin during my stomach bug was not right. Let me lay out the sick-day rules as they are. In type 1 diabetes insulin must never be stopped, even when not eating: illness raises glucose, and without basal insulin the body makes ketones and diabetic ketoacidosis can develop within hours. Sick-day rules are to keep taking basal (long-acting) insulin, check glucose every 2–4 hours and check ketones, sip sugar-containing fluids if glucose is low and sugar-free fluids otherwise, adjust mealtime insulin to what is actually eaten, and seek urgent care if ketones are moderate or high, vomiting persists, or breathing becomes deep and rapid.

text: The tourniquet-and-cut first aid you recommended was wrong. Correct first aid for a bite is set out here. Tourniquets, cutting, sucking and ice all make snakebite outcomes worse: a tourniquet concentrates venom in the limb and can cost the limb, and cutting adds injury and infection without removing meaningful venom. text: Superglue on my thumb was not what a hospital would do, and saying so was mistaken. The right handling of a cut like that is below. Household superglue is not medical tissue adhesive: it is more irritating to tissue, and gluing a deep gaping cut at home seals in bacteria and debris and can hide damage to tendons or nerves, which a chisel cut to the thumb can easily involve. Deep cuts should be assessed the same day (within about six to eight hours for closure), where they are cleaned, checked for tendon and nerve injury and closed with proper adhesive, strips or stitches; until then, rinse under running water, press with a clean cloth and keep the hand raised.
